Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ১) Which one is known as cell suicide?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Apoptosis is known as “programmed cell death” or “cell suicide.” It is a regulated process in which unwanted or damaged cells are eliminated without causing significant surrounding inflammation.

  • Apoptosis → cell suicide 

  • Necrosis → uncontrolled/pathological cell death

  • Atresia → developmental degeneration/closure of a normal anatomical structure

  • Aplasia → failure of development of an organ or tissue

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Term Key concept
Apoptosis Programmed cell death / cell suicide
Necrosis Pathological cell death
Atresia Failure/degeneration of a lumen or structure
Aplasia Failure of organ development

Exam Pearl:
Apoptosis = programmed cell death = “cell suicide.”

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ২) Which one is not secreted by kidney?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The kidney secretes or produces several important substances:

  • Erythropoietin (EPO) → produced by renal interstitial cells; stimulates RBC production.

  • 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (Calcitriol) → active vitamin D, formed by renal 1α-hydroxylase.

  • Renin → secreted by juxtaglomerular cells.

  • Angiotensin → not secreted by the kidney. Angiotensin I/II are generated in the RAAS cascade, mainly through enzymatic conversion of angiotensinogen by renin and ACE.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Kidney → EPO + Renin + Calcitriol

  • Angiotensinogen → liver

  • Renin → kidney

  • ACE → mainly pulmonary endothelium

  • Angiotensin II → formed by ACE

Exam Pearl:
Kidney secretes renin, not angiotensin.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৩) Which is example of positive feedback?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Blood clotting (coagulation) is a classic example of positive feedback, where the initial activation of clotting factors leads to further activation of additional clotting factors, rapidly amplifying the response until the clot is formed.

  • Blood clotting → Positive feedback ✅

  • BP control → Negative feedback

  • Temperature regulation → Negative feedback

  • Acid–base balance → Negative feedback

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Positive feedback: Blood clotting, childbirth (oxytocin)

  • Negative feedback: BP, temperature, blood glucose, acid–base balance

Exam Pearl:
Blood clotting = classic positive feedback mechanism.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৪) Most of the oxygen in blood is carried in which form?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
About 98–99% of oxygen in blood is transported bound to hemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin. Only about 1–2% is carried dissolved in plasma.

  • Oxyhemoglobin → ~98–99% ✅

  • Dissolved in plasma → ~1–2%

  • Carboxyhemoglobin → hemoglobin bound to CO

  • Methemoglobin → oxidized hemoglobin (Fe³⁺), cannot effectively bind O₂

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • O₂ → mainly oxyhemoglobin

  • CO₂ → mainly bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻)

  • CO → carboxyhemoglobin

Exam Pearl:
Most blood O₂ is carried as oxyhemoglobin.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৫) Which one is limiting pH of urine?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The lowest (limiting) pH of urine is approximately 4.5. Even when the body needs to excrete a large acid load, urine pH normally cannot fall below about 4.5 because of the limits of free H⁺ secretion.

  • 4.5 → minimum urine pH ✅

  • 5.0, 5.5 → can occur normally but are not the limiting value.

  • 4.0 → below the normal physiological minimum.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Normal urine pH → approximately 4.5–8.0

  • Minimum urine pH → 4.5

  • Urine can become more acidic during metabolic acidosis.

Exam Pearl:
Limiting urine pH = 4.5.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৬) What is the main component of cell membrane?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The cell membrane is mainly composed of lipids, particularly phospholipids, arranged as a phospholipid bilayer. Proteins are embedded within this bilayer and are essential for transport, receptors, enzymes, and signaling.

  • Lipid → main structural component ✅

  • Protein → major functional component

  • Carbohydrate → mainly attached to lipids/proteins as glycolipids/glycoproteins

  • Cholesterol → regulates membrane fluidity

Exam Pearl:
Cell membrane = phospholipid bilayer + proteins + cholesterol + carbohydrat

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৭) Which one is normal GFR value?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The normal glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in a healthy adult is approximately 125 mL/min, equivalent to about 180 L/day.

  • 125 mL/min → normal GFR ✅

  • 130, 145, 150 mL/min → above the standard reference value.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • GFR → ~125 mL/min

  • Daily filtrate → ~180 L/day

  • Renal plasma flow → ~600 mL/min

  • Renal blood flow → ~1,200 mL/min

Exam Pearl:
Normal GFR = 125 mL/min ≈ 180 L/day.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৮) Which is not a characteristics of oxygen hemoglobin dissociation curve?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.option3: curve is almost flat when PO2 is above 100 mmHg
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Explanation:
The oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve is reversible, because oxygen can bind to hemoglobin in the lungs and dissociate from it in the tissues.

The other statements are characteristic features:

  • Sigmoid-shaped → due to cooperative binding of O₂ to hemoglobin 

  • Begins from the origin (0,0) → essentially true for the standard curve 

  • Plateaus above PO₂ ~60–100 mmHg → represents high Hb saturation despite further increases in PO₂ 

  • Irreversible → incorrect 

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Shape → Sigmoid

  • Lungs → O₂ loading

  • Tissues → O₂ unloading

  • Right shift → ↑ O₂ unloading

  • Left shift → ↑ O₂ affinity

Exam Pearl:
O₂–Hb binding is reversible; therefore “irreversible” is NOT a characteristic.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৯) Which is example of primary active transport?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump is the classic example of primary active transport. It directly uses energy from ATP hydrolysis to transport ions against their electrochemical gradients. For every ATP molecule hydrolyzed, it transports 3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ into the cell. This pump is essential for maintaining the resting membrane potential, cell volume, and the Na⁺ gradient that drives several secondary active transport processes. In contrast, the sodium-glucose cotransporter is a secondary active transport mechanism because it uses the Na⁺ gradient indirectly generated by Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Na⁺/H⁺ and Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange mechanisms are also secondary active transport processes.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Primary active transport: Directly uses ATP.

  • Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase: 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in per ATP.

  • Na⁺-glucose cotransporter: Secondary active transport.

  • Na⁺/H⁺ exchanger: Secondary active transport.

  • Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger: Secondary active transport.

Exam Pearl:
Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is the classic example of primary active transport.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ১০) Which one is secreted by PCT?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) is the major site for both reabsorption and secretion of various substances. Urate (uric acid) is secreted by the PCT through organic anion transport systems, although it also undergoes substantial reabsorption, making its overall renal handling complex. PAH (para-aminohippuric acid) is also actively secreted by the PCT and is a classic marker used to estimate effective renal plasma flow. However, if the question asks which substance is characteristically secreted by the PCT among these options, urate is the accepted answer. Cl⁻ is predominantly reabsorbed, while HCO₃⁻ is also predominantly reabsorbed in the PCT.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • PCT secretes H⁺, urate, PAH, and organic acids/bases.

  • PCT reabsorbs approximately 80–90% of filtered HCO₃⁻.

  • PAH is actively secreted by PCT.

  • Chloride is mainly reabsorbed in the PCT.

  • Urate undergoes both reabsorption and secretion.

Exam Pearl:
PCT is the major tubular site for secretion of PAH and urate.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ১১) Which is not a feature of facilitated diffusion?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Facilitated diffusion is a form of passive transport in which substances move down their concentration or electrochemical gradient through specific membrane proteins, such as channels or carrier proteins. It does not require metabolic energy (ATP). Because the driving force is the concentration/electrochemical gradient, the net movement can be bidirectional depending on which side has the higher concentration. A membrane protein is essential for facilitated diffusion; therefore, the statement “membrane isn't must” is also poorly worded. However, among the options, movement against the concentration gradient is the clearest feature that is not compatible with facilitated diffusion and therefore is the best exam answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Facilitated diffusion is passive transport.

  • Moves down the concentration/electrochemical gradient.

  • No ATP is required.

  • Requires a membrane protein: channel or carrier.

  • It is selective and may show saturation.

Exam Pearl:
Facilitated diffusion = protein-mediated, no ATP, down the gradient.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ১২) Most of the CO2 is transported in blood in which form?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Most carbon dioxide (CO₂) produced by tissues is transported in the blood as bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻). Approximately 70% of CO₂ is transported in this form. Within red blood cells, carbonic anhydrase rapidly catalyzes the conversion of CO₂ and water into carbonic acid, which dissociates into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻. The bicarbonate then moves into plasma in exchange for chloride ions, a process called the chloride shift. About 20–23% of CO₂ is transported as carbamino compounds, mainly carbaminohemoglobin, while only about 7–10% is physically dissolved in plasma. “Carbomino protein” is not the standard term used for the major physiological form.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • About 70% CO₂ → bicarbonate.

  • About 20–23% → carbamino compounds.

  • About 7–10% → dissolved CO₂.

  • Carbonic anhydrase is abundant in RBCs.

  • Bicarbonate transport involves the chloride shift.

Exam Pearl:
Most CO₂ is transported as plasma bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻).

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ১৩) Which metabolic pathway occurs in kidney?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The kidney, particularly the renal cortex, is an important site of gluconeogenesis, especially during prolonged fasting. Although the liver is the major organ responsible for gluconeogenesis under normal conditions, the kidney contributes significantly during prolonged fasting and metabolic acidosis. Renal gluconeogenesis also helps generate ammonia (NH₃) from glutamine, which facilitates acid excretion and maintenance of acid–base balance. Glycogenesis is not a major characteristic metabolic function of the kidney. Beta-oxidation does occur in renal tissues, but it is not the classic single-best answer for this question. The urea cycle is primarily a hepatic pathway; the kidney does not possess the complete urea cycle.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Kidney is an important site of gluconeogenesis.

  • Renal gluconeogenesis increases during prolonged fasting.

  • Kidney metabolizes glutamine → NH₃, aiding acid excretion.

  • Urea cycle: primarily liver.

  • Gluconeogenesis: mainly liver, with significant renal contribution.

Exam Pearl:
Kidney = important extrahepatic site of gluconeogenesis, especially during prolonged fasting.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ১৪) Which plasma protein has site of origin other than liver?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Most plasma proteins are synthesized in the liver, including albumin, fibrinogen, and prothrombin. However, globulins have an important site of origin outside the liver. Specifically, immunoglobulins (antibodies), which constitute the gamma-globulin fraction, are produced by plasma cells derived from B lymphocytes. Other globulin proteins are synthesized in the liver, so “globulin” is a broad category; nevertheless, in standard examination questions, it is the best answer because the immunoglobulin fraction is produced by plasma cells rather than hepatocytes.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Albumin: synthesized by liver.

  • Fibrinogen: synthesized by liver.

  • Prothrombin: synthesized by liver.

  • Immunoglobulins: produced by plasma cells.

  • Gamma globulins mainly consist of immunoglobulins.

Exam Pearl:
Immunoglobulins are the major plasma proteins produced outside the liver, by plasma cells.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ১৫) Macula densa is present in-
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The macula densa is a specialized group of epithelial cells located in the early distal convoluted tubule (DCT), where the DCT comes into close contact with the vascular pole of the same nephron. It forms an important component of the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) along with juxtaglomerular cells and extraglomerular mesangial cells. Macula densa cells sense the tubular NaCl concentration, mainly through the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter (NKCC2), and participate in tubuloglomerular feedback and regulation of renin release. The loop of Henle, afferent arteriole, and Bowman's capsule do not contain the macula densa.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Macula densa → early DCT.

  • Part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus.

  • Senses tubular NaCl.

  • Important in tubuloglomerular feedback.

  • Communicates with juxtaglomerular cells to regulate renin release.

Exam Pearl:
Macula densa = specialized cells of the early DCT at the vascular pole of the nephron.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ১৬) Haldane effect depends on...... in blood?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The Haldane effect describes how oxygenation of hemoglobin in the lungs promotes the release of CO₂ and H⁺ from blood, thereby facilitating CO₂ excretion. Conversely, deoxygenated hemoglobin in peripheral tissues has a greater capacity to bind CO₂ and H⁺, facilitating CO₂ uptake. Therefore, the Haldane effect primarily depends on the oxygenation state of hemoglobin, which is reflected by PO₂. This is distinct from the Bohr effect, in which increased CO₂/H⁺ reduces hemoglobin's affinity for O₂. Thus, among the given options, PO₂ is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Haldane effect: O₂ loading promotes CO₂ unloading.

  • Depends mainly on hemoglobin oxygenation (PO₂).

  • Deoxygenated Hb carries more CO₂ and H⁺.

  • Bohr effect: CO₂/H⁺ promotes O₂ unloading.

  • Haldane effect is especially important in the lungs.

Exam Pearl:
Haldane effect = oxygenation of Hb facilitates CO₂ unloading.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ১৭) Which is a maturation factor for erythropoiesis?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Folic acid (vitamin B9) is a key maturation factor required for normal erythropoiesis. Along with vitamin B12, it is essential for DNA synthesis during erythroblast maturation. Deficiency impairs nuclear maturation and produces megaloblastic anemia, characterized by ineffective erythropoiesis and megaloblasts in the bone marrow. Iron is primarily required for hemoglobin synthesis, so it is considered an erythropoietic/hemoglobinization factor rather than the classic maturation factor. Essential amino acids are needed for general protein synthesis, while vitamin C facilitates iron absorption but is not classified as the principal maturation factor.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Maturation factors: Vitamin B12 and folate.

  • Both are essential for DNA synthesis.

  • Deficiency → megaloblastic anemia.

  • Iron → hemoglobin synthesis.

  • Vitamin C → enhances iron absorption.

Exam Pearl:
Folate and vitamin B12 are the classic maturation factors for erythropoiesis.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ১৮) ACE is present in........?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) is widely distributed in vascular endothelial cells but is particularly abundant in the pulmonary capillary endothelium. As blood passes through the pulmonary circulation, ACE converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II by removing two amino acids from angiotensin I. ACE also degrades bradykinin, contributing to vasoconstriction and blood pressure regulation. Although ACE is present in several tissues, including the kidneys and other vascular beds, the lungs are the classic exam answer because of their extensive endothelial surface area and major role in circulating ACE activity.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • ACE is abundant in pulmonary vascular endothelium.

  • Converts Angiotensin I → Angiotensin II.

  • Degrades bradykinin.

  • Angiotensin II → vasoconstriction and aldosterone secretion.

  • ACE inhibitors increase bradykinin → dry cough and sometimes angioedema.

Exam Pearl:
ACE: classically associated with pulmonary capillary endothelium.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ১৯) Which is an abnormal hemoglobin?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Hb-S (sickle hemoglobin) is an abnormal/variant hemoglobin caused by a point mutation in the β-globin gene, in which valine replaces glutamic acid at position 6 of the β-chain. Under low-oxygen conditions, Hb-S polymerizes, causing red cells to become sickle-shaped and leading to hemolysis and vaso-occlusive complications in sickle cell disease. Hb-A is the normal predominant adult hemoglobin, while Hb-A₂ is a normal minor adult hemoglobin composed of α₂δ₂ chains. Hb-F (α₂γ₂) is the predominant hemoglobin during fetal life and is also normally present in small amounts after birth.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hb-A: α₂β₂; major adult Hb.

  • Hb-A₂: α₂δ₂; normally about 2–3.5%.

  • Hb-F: α₂γ₂; predominant fetal Hb.

  • Hb-S: abnormal variant Hb.

  • Hb-S mutation: β6 Glu → Val.

Exam Pearl:
Hb-S is the classic abnormal hemoglobin causing sickle cell disease.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ২০) Which respiratory center controls rate & depth of breathing?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The pneumotaxic center, located in the upper pons, helps regulate the rate and depth of breathing by controlling the duration of inspiration. It sends inhibitory impulses to the inspiratory center, thereby limiting inspiration. A stronger pneumotaxic signal shortens inspiration, resulting in increased respiratory rate and decreased tidal volume. Conversely, reduced pneumotaxic activity allows longer inspiration and deeper breaths. The inspiratory center in the medulla generates the basic inspiratory rhythm, while the apneustic center promotes prolonged inspiration. Therefore, among the given options, the pneumotaxic center is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Pneumotaxic center: regulates rate and depth of breathing.

  • Located in the upper pons.

  • Inhibits inspiration and limits inspiratory duration.

  • Strong pneumotaxic activity → rapid, shallow breathing.

  • Apneustic center → promotes prolonged inspiration.

Exam Pearl:
Pneumotaxic center acts as the “inspiratory switch-off” center and regulates respiratory rate and depth.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ২১) Podocytes are present in.......?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Podocytes are highly specialized epithelial cells that form the visceral layer of Bowman’s capsule and cover the outer surface of the glomerular capillaries. Their cytoplasmic extensions, called primary processes and foot processes (pedicels), interdigitate around the glomerular capillaries and form filtration slits bridged by slit diaphragms. Together with the fenestrated glomerular endothelium and glomerular basement membrane, podocytes form the glomerular filtration barrier. Therefore, podocytes are located on the outer surface of the glomerular capillary loops, not within the afferent arteriole or peritubular capillaries.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Podocytes = visceral epithelial cells of Bowman’s capsule.

  • Cover the outer surface of glomerular capillaries.

  • Foot processes → filtration slits.

  • Slit diaphragm is an important component of the filtration barrier.

  • Damage to podocytes can cause proteinuria.

Exam Pearl:
Podocytes cover the outer surface of glomerular capillaries and form the visceral layer of Bowman’s capsule.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ২২) Which leukocyte has horse shoe type nucleus?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
A monocyte characteristically has a large, abundant cytoplasm and a kidney-shaped or horseshoe-shaped nucleus. It is the largest normal circulating leukocyte and typically has fine azurophilic granules. After migrating into tissues, monocytes differentiate primarily into macrophages and related phagocytic cells. Neutrophils have a multilobed nucleus, usually with 3–5 lobes. Eosinophils have a characteristic bilobed nucleus with prominent eosinophilic granules, while basophils have a lobed or S-shaped nucleus that is often obscured by coarse basophilic granules.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Monocyte: kidney/horse-shoe-shaped nucleus.

  • Neutrophil: multilobed nucleus.

  • Eosinophil: bilobed nucleus.

  • Basophil: lobed/S-shaped nucleus, coarse granules.

  • Monocytes differentiate into macrophages in tissues.

Exam Pearl:
Horse-shoe or kidney-shaped nucleus = Monocyte.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ২৩) Glomerular membrane is formed by all of the following except......?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The glomerular filtration barrier is formed by three main components: fenestrated glomerular endothelium, the glomerular basement membrane (GBM), and the visceral epithelial cells (podocytes) with their interdigitating foot processes and slit diaphragms. These layers together determine the selective filtration of water and small solutes while restricting blood cells and most plasma proteins. Mesangial cells are located between the glomerular capillary loops and provide structural support, regulate capillary surface area, and have phagocytic and contractile functions. However, they are not a component of the glomerular filtration membrane. Therefore, mesangial cell is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Filtration barrier: endothelium + GBM + podocytes.

  • Endothelium → prevents blood cell passage.

  • GBM → major barrier to plasma proteins.

  • Podocyte foot processes → form filtration slits.

  • Mesangial cells → support and regulate glomerular capillaries.

Exam Pearl:
Glomerular filtration barrier = fenestrated endothelium + GBM + podocyte slit diaphragm; mesangial cells are not part of it.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ২৪) Which nerve is related to Hering-Breuer reflex?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The Hering–Breuer inflation reflex is mediated by the vagus nerve (CN X). Pulmonary stretch receptors located mainly in the smooth muscle of the airways are activated when the lungs become excessively inflated. Their afferent impulses travel through the vagus nerve to the respiratory centers in the medulla, where they inhibit further inspiration. This protective reflex helps prevent overinflation of the lungs, particularly during large tidal volumes. The glossopharyngeal nerve carries sensory information from the carotid sinus and carotid bodies, while the trigeminal and facial nerves are not responsible for the Hering–Breuer reflex.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hering–Breuer reflex → Vagus nerve (CN X).

  • Receptor → pulmonary stretch receptor.

  • Afferent pathway → vagus.

  • Effect → inhibits inspiration.

  • Important mainly during large tidal volumes, especially in infants.

Exam Pearl:
Hering–Breuer inflation reflex = pulmonary stretch receptor → vagus nerve → inhibition of inspiration.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ২৫) What is second line defense against infection?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
In the classical description of the body's second line of defense, neutrophils are rapidly recruited from the blood to sites of infection and perform phagocytosis and killing of microorganisms. They are especially important in acute bacterial infections. Tissue macrophages are considered an earlier cellular defense because they are already present in tissues and can phagocytose invading organisms before large numbers of neutrophils arrive. Monocytes circulate in blood and later migrate into tissues, where they differentiate into macrophages. Basophils participate mainly in allergic and inflammatory responses and are not regarded as the principal second-line phagocytic defense.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • First line → physical and chemical barriers such as skin and mucosa.

  • Tissue macrophages → early/first cellular defense.

  • Neutrophils → major second-line phagocytic defense.

  • Monocytes → migrate into tissues and become macrophages.

  • Basophils → mainly involved in hypersensitivity/allergic reactions.

Exam Pearl:
Neutrophils are the classic second-line cellular defense against invading microorganisms.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ২৬) Which hormone increases GFR?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Prostaglandins, particularly PGE₂ and PGI₂, promote afferent arteriolar vasodilation, helping maintain renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate (GFR), especially when renal perfusion is threatened by vasoconstrictors. In contrast, norepinephrine causes renal vasoconstriction and decreases GFR. Endothelin is a potent vasoconstrictor that reduces renal blood flow and generally decreases GFR. Angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole at physiological concentrations, helping maintain GFR during reduced renal perfusion; however, at high concentrations it also constricts the afferent arteriole and can reduce renal blood flow and GFR. Thus, prostaglandin is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • PGE₂/PGI₂ → afferent vasodilation → supports GFR.

  • Norepinephrine → renal vasoconstriction → decreases GFR.

  • Endothelin → potent vasoconstrictor → decreases GFR.

  • Angiotensin II → preferential efferent constriction at moderate levels.

  • NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandins and can reduce renal perfusion, especially in susceptible patients.

Exam Pearl:
Prostaglandins increase/maintain GFR mainly by dilating the afferent arteriole.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ২৭) What is the location of microglia?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Microglia are the resident immune cells of the central nervous system (CNS) and are found throughout the brain and spinal cord. They are specialized macrophage-like cells derived from yolk-sac progenitors and are responsible for immune surveillance, phagocytosis of cellular debris, and responses to injury or infection within the CNS. They are distinct from astrocytes and oligodendrocytes, which are other major glial cell types. The liver contains Kupffer cells, the kidney contains resident macrophage populations, and the skin contains immune cells including Langerhans cells. Therefore, the best answer is the brain.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Microglia → CNS.

  • Function → phagocytosis and immune surveillance.

  • Microglia are the resident macrophage-like cells of the CNS.

  • Kupffer cells → liver.

  • Langerhans cells → epidermis.

Exam Pearl:
Microglia = resident macrophages of the CNS.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ২৮) Which is the cause of stagnant hypoxia?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Stagnant hypoxia, also called circulatory hypoxia, occurs when tissue blood flow is reduced despite adequate arterial oxygen content. This results in inadequate oxygen delivery to tissues because of reduced cardiac output or impaired circulation. Congestive cardiac failure (CCF) is a classic cause because reduced cardiac output decreases tissue perfusion, producing stagnant hypoxia. Asthma and pneumonia primarily cause hypoxic/hypoxemic hypoxia through impaired ventilation or gas exchange. Cyanide poisoning causes histotoxic hypoxia, in which tissues are unable to utilize oxygen despite adequate oxygen delivery. Therefore, CCF is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Stagnant/circulatory hypoxia → reduced tissue blood flow.

  • Classic cause → CCF/shock.

  • Asthma → mainly hypoxemic hypoxia.

  • Pneumonia → mainly hypoxemic hypoxia.

  • Cyanide poisoning → histotoxic hypoxia.

Exam Pearl:
Stagnant hypoxia = inadequate tissue perfusion; think CCF or shock.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ২৯) The value of Net filtration pressure is.......... mmHg?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The normal net filtration pressure (NFP) across the glomerular filtration barrier is approximately 20 mmHg. It is determined by the balance between the forces favoring filtration and those opposing it. The main force favoring filtration is glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (≈60 mmHg). The major opposing forces are Bowman’s capsule hydrostatic pressure (≈18 mmHg) and glomerular capillary colloid osmotic pressure (≈32 mmHg). Bowman’s space colloid osmotic pressure is normally negligible because very little protein is filtered. Therefore: NFP = 60 − (18 + 32) = 10 mmHg, not 20 mmHg. Thus, the question's options conflict with the standard calculation; 10 mmHg is the accepted physiological value.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Normal GFR ≈ 125 mL/min.

  • Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure ≈ 60 mmHg.

  • Bowman’s capsule hydrostatic pressure ≈ 18 mmHg.

  • Glomerular capillary oncotic pressure ≈ 32 mmHg.

  • NFP ≈ 10 mmHg.

Exam Pearl:
Normal glomerular NFP is approximately 10 mmHg, so option ক is the correct answer.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৩০) How many basic events occur in hemostasis?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Hemostasis is classically described as occurring through three basic events: vascular spasm (vasoconstriction), platelet plug formation, and blood coagulation. Immediately after vascular injury, vasoconstriction reduces blood loss. Platelets then adhere to the damaged vessel wall, become activated, and aggregate to form a temporary platelet plug. Subsequently, the coagulation cascade generates thrombin, which converts fibrinogen into fibrin, stabilizing the platelet plug and producing a more durable clot. Although modern descriptions may separately discuss clot retraction and fibrinolysis as later processes, the classic examination classification of the basic events of hemostasis consists of three stages.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

    1. Vascular spasm → immediate vasoconstriction.

    1. Platelet plug formation → primary hemostasis.

    1. Coagulation → fibrin clot formation (secondary hemostasis).

  • Platelet plug = primary hemostasis.

  • Fibrin formation = secondary hemostasis.

Exam Pearl:
Classic hemostasis has 3 basic events: vascular spasm → platelet plug → coagulation.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৩১) Which of the following segment of a nephron is impermeable to water?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle is classically impermeable to water. It actively reabsorbs Na⁺, K⁺, and Cl⁻ through the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ (NKCC2) cotransporter without accompanying water movement. Therefore, it is called the diluting segment and plays a major role in establishing the medullary osmotic gradient. The thin descending limb is highly permeable to water, while the PCT is also highly water-permeable. The early DCT has relatively low water permeability, but in standard single-best-answer questions, the thick ascending limb is the classic answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Thick ascending limb → impermeable to water.

  • NKCC2 → Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻ reabsorption.

  • Called the diluting segment.

  • Thin descending limb → highly permeable to water.

  • PCT → highly permeable to water.

Exam Pearl:
Thick ascending limb = “water impermeable, salt reabsorbing” segment of the nephron.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৩২) Oxygen therapy is mostly effective in which type of hypoxia?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Oxygen therapy is most effective in hypoxic (hypoxemic) hypoxia, where arterial PO₂ is reduced. Increasing the inspired oxygen concentration raises alveolar and arterial PO₂, thereby increasing the amount of oxygen available for tissue delivery. In anemic hypoxia, arterial PO₂ is usually normal, but oxygen-carrying capacity is reduced because of decreased hemoglobin, so oxygen therapy has limited benefit. In stagnant (circulatory) hypoxia, tissue perfusion is inadequate despite adequate arterial oxygen. In histotoxic hypoxia, such as cyanide poisoning, tissues cannot utilize oxygen despite adequate oxygen delivery. Therefore, hypoxic hypoxia responds best to oxygen therapy.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hypoxic hypoxia: decreased arterial PO₂ → oxygen therapy highly effective.

  • Anemic hypoxia → decreased Hb/O₂ content.

  • Stagnant hypoxia → decreased tissue perfusion.

  • Histotoxic hypoxia → impaired cellular O₂ utilization.

  • Cyanide poisoning → histotoxic hypoxia.

Exam Pearl:
Oxygen therapy is most effective in hypoxic/hypoxemic hypoxia.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৩৩) vWF is related to which clotting factor?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Von Willebrand factor (vWF) is closely associated with factor VIII (antihemophilic factor A). vWF is produced mainly by endothelial cells and megakaryocytes and circulates in plasma bound to factor VIII. It has two major roles: it mediates platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelial structures at sites of vascular injury and stabilizes factor VIII by protecting it from premature degradation in plasma. Deficiency or dysfunction of vWF causes von Willebrand disease, characterized primarily by impaired primary hemostasis and, in some cases, reduced factor VIII activity. Factor IX is antihemophilic factor B, while factors V and VII are unrelated to vWF.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • vWF is associated with Factor VIII.

  • vWF mediates platelet adhesion.

  • vWF stabilizes and protects Factor VIII.

  • vWF deficiency → von Willebrand disease.

  • Factor VIII → Antihemophilic factor A.

  • Factor IX → Christmas factor / Antihemophilic factor B.

Exam Pearl:
vWF carries and stabilizes Factor VIII and mediates platelet adhesion.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৩৪) Which one has highest capacity of reabsorption?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) has the greatest capacity for tubular reabsorption. It reabsorbs approximately 65% of filtered Na⁺ and water, along with nearly all filtered glucose and amino acids under normal conditions. It also reabsorbs a large proportion of filtered HCO₃⁻, phosphate, and potassium. The PCT has a large surface area due to its extensive brush border, abundant mitochondria, and high permeability to water. The loop of Henle, DCT, and collecting duct perform important selective functions but have a lower overall reabsorptive capacity compared with the PCT.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • PCT → maximum bulk reabsorption.

  • About 65% of filtered Na⁺ and water reabsorbed.

  • Nearly 100% glucose and amino acids normally reabsorbed.

  • About 80–90% HCO₃⁻ reabsorbed in PCT.

  • PCT has a prominent brush border.

Exam Pearl:
PCT is the major site of bulk reabsorption in the nephron.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৩৫) Which is not vitamin K dependent clotting factor?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The vitamin K–dependent clotting factors are II, VII, IX, and X. In the options, prothrombin (factor II), stable factor (factor VII), and Christmas factor (factor IX) are therefore vitamin K dependent. Labile factor (factor V) is not vitamin K dependent. Vitamin K is required in the liver for γ-carboxylation of specific glutamate residues on factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as proteins C and S, allowing them to bind calcium and participate effectively in coagulation. Factor V is a cofactor in the prothrombinase complex but does not undergo vitamin K–dependent γ-carboxylation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Vitamin K–dependent factors: II, VII, IX, X.

  • Also vitamin K dependent: Protein C and Protein S.

  • Factor V = labile factor → not vitamin K dependent.

  • Factor II → prothrombin.

  • Factor VII → stable factor.

  • Factor IX → Christmas factor.

Exam Pearl:
Vitamin K factors = 1972: X, IX, VII, II; Factor V is not vitamin K dependent.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৩৬) Which is a restrictive airway disease?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Pleural effusion causes a restrictive ventilatory defect by accumulating fluid in the pleural space, which limits lung expansion and reduces lung volumes, particularly total lung capacity (TLC) and vital capacity. In restrictive disease, the primary problem is difficulty expanding the lungs or chest wall, rather than increased airway resistance. Asthma and chronic bronchitis are obstructive airway diseases characterized by increased airway resistance. Emphysema is also an obstructive disease, caused by destruction of alveolar walls and loss of elastic recoil. Therefore, among the given options, pleural effusion is the best example of restrictive lung disease.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Restrictive disease → ↓ TLC, ↓ FVC.

  • Pleural effusion → restrictive ventilatory defect.

  • Asthma → obstructive.

  • Chronic bronchitis → obstructive.

  • Emphysema → obstructive.

  • Obstructive disease → typically ↓ FEV₁/FVC.

Exam Pearl:
Pleural effusion is restrictive; asthma, chronic bronchitis, and emphysema are obstructive.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৩৭) Obligatory urine output is.......mL/day?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The obligatory urine volume is the minimum amount of urine required to excrete the daily osmotic load while maintaining normal plasma osmolality. The kidneys can maximally concentrate urine to approximately 1200 mOsm/L. With an average daily solute load of about 600 mOsm/day, the minimum urine volume required is approximately 500 mL/day. This value is therefore commonly used in physiology and medical entrance examinations as the obligatory urine output in a healthy adult. It is important to distinguish this from normal daily urine output, which is roughly 1–2 L/day. A urine output below about 400–500 mL/day is considered markedly reduced.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Obligatory urine volume ≈ 500 mL/day.

  • Maximum urine concentration ≈ 1200 mOsm/L.

  • Average daily osmotic load ≈ 600 mOsm/day.

  • Normal adult urine output ≈ 1–2 L/day.

  • Obligatory volume prevents accumulation of metabolic waste.

Exam Pearl:
Obligatory urine output = approximately 500 mL/day.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৩৮) Extrinsic pathway for blood coagulation is initiated by activation of factor......?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The extrinsic pathway of coagulation is initiated by exposure of tissue factor (Factor III) following tissue injury. Tissue factor binds to and activates Factor VII, forming the tissue factor–VIIa complex. This complex rapidly activates Factor X (and also Factor IX), thereby entering the common pathway. Activated Factor X combines with Factor V, phospholipid, and calcium to form the prothrombinase complex, which converts prothrombin to thrombin. Therefore, among the given options, Factor X is the best answer if the question asks for the factor through which the extrinsic pathway proceeds into the common pathway. Strictly speaking, the pathway is initiated by activation of Factor VII, which is not provided as an option.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Extrinsic pathway trigger → Tissue factor (Factor III).

  • Tissue factor activates Factor VII.

  • TF–VIIa complex → activates Factor X.

  • Factor X → common pathway.

  • Common pathway: X → V → II → I.

Exam Pearl:
Extrinsic pathway starts with Factor VII; among these options, Factor X is the correct downstream entry into the common pathway.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৩৯) What is the maximum osmolarity in counter current mechanism?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The maximum osmolarity of the renal medullary interstitium generated by the counter-current multiplication system is approximately 1200 mOsm/L in a normal adult. This high osmolarity is established mainly by the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, which actively reabsorbs Na⁺, K⁺, and Cl⁻ while being impermeable to water. The counter-current multiplier progressively increases the osmotic gradient from the cortex toward the inner medulla. In the presence of ADH, the collecting ducts become highly permeable to water, allowing water to leave the tubular fluid along this medullary gradient and producing concentrated urine. Therefore, 1200 mOsm/L is the standard exam answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Maximum medullary osmolarity → 1200 mOsm/L.

  • Thick ascending limb → salt reabsorption, water impermeable.

  • Counter-current multiplier → loop of Henle.

  • ADH → increases collecting duct water permeability.

  • Maximum urine concentration → approximately 1200 mOsm/L.

Exam Pearl:
Maximum renal medullary osmolarity = 1200 mOsm/L.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৪০) Reduced oxygen in blood is called......?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Hypoxaemia means an abnormally low oxygen level in arterial blood, usually reflected by a reduced arterial PO₂ (PaO₂). It is different from hypoxia, which refers to inadequate oxygen availability or utilization at the tissue level. Hypoxaemia can cause hypoxic hypoxia when arterial oxygen content and tissue oxygen delivery become insufficient. Anoxia refers to an extreme or near-complete absence of oxygen at the tissue level, while hypercapnia means an increased arterial CO₂ level (PaCO₂). Therefore, when the question specifically asks about reduced oxygen in blood, the best answer is hypoxaemia.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hypoxaemia → low O₂ in arterial blood.

  • Hypoxia → inadequate O₂ at tissue level.

  • Anoxia → severe/near-complete lack of tissue O₂.

  • Hypercapnia → increased arterial CO₂.

  • Hypoxaemia is commonly assessed by PaO₂ and oxygen saturation.

Exam Pearl:
Reduced oxygen in arterial blood = hypoxaemia; reduced tissue oxygen = hypoxia.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৪১) Which is not a complication of massive blood transfusion?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Massive blood transfusion can cause several metabolic and cardiopulmonary complications, including hyperkalemia, citrate toxicity, and pulmonary edema. Stored red blood cells gradually accumulate potassium, so rapid transfusion can produce hyperkalemia. Citrate used as an anticoagulant binds calcium and may cause hypocalcemia, particularly with rapid or massive transfusion. Volume overload can lead to pulmonary edema. Air embolism, however, is not a typical complication of massive blood transfusion itself. It is more associated with inappropriate infusion techniques or central venous procedures. Therefore, air embolism is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Massive transfusion → hyperkalemia.

  • Citrate toxicity → hypocalcemia.

  • Rapid volume loading → pulmonary edema.

  • Stored blood → increased extracellular K⁺.

  • Hypothermia and dilutional coagulopathy may also occur.

Exam Pearl:
Massive transfusion complications include hyperkalemia, citrate-induced hypocalcemia, hypothermia, and volume overload; air embolism is not a classic complication.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৪২) Blood is detected in urine by which test?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The orthotolidine test is a chemical test used to detect blood/hemoglobin in urine. Hemoglobin and myoglobin have peroxidase-like activity that catalyzes oxidation of orthotolidine, producing a characteristic color change. Therefore, the test can detect hematuria as well as hemoglobinuria and may also react with myoglobin. Rothera’s test is used mainly for detecting ketone bodies in urine. Fouchet’s test is used for detecting bilirubin. Hay’s sulfur test detects bile salts based on their ability to reduce the surface tension of urine. Hence, orthotolidine is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Orthotolidine test → blood/hemoglobin in urine.

  • Rothera’s test → ketone bodies.

  • Fouchet’s test → bilirubin.

  • Hay’s test → bile salts.

  • Urine dipstick for blood detects heme peroxidase activity.

Exam Pearl:
Orthotolidine = blood in urine; Rothera = ketones; Fouchet = bilirubin; Hay = bile salts.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৪৩) Heart muscle cannot be fatigued due to its.......?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Cardiac muscle normally does not undergo fatigue or tetanic contraction because of its long refractory period. The cardiac action potential has a prolonged plateau phase, largely due to Ca²⁺ influx through L-type calcium channels, which extends the absolute refractory period. This refractory period overlaps almost the entire duration of the cardiac contraction, preventing a second action potential from being initiated before relaxation occurs. Consequently, cardiac muscle cannot undergo summation or tetanus, allowing the heart to relax and refill between contractions. This property is essential for continuous rhythmic pumping. Contractility and excitability are important properties of cardiac muscle but are not the primary reason it cannot be tetanized.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Cardiac muscle has a long refractory period.

  • Long refractory period → prevents summation and tetanus.

  • Plateau phase mainly due to Ca²⁺ influx through L-type channels.

  • Skeletal muscle has a short refractory period → can undergo tetanus.

  • Cardiac muscle must relax between contractions for ventricular filling.

Exam Pearl:
Long refractory period prevents tetanus and protects the heart from sustained contraction.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৪৪) Which is never spared in central cyanosis?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.option3: nail bed tip of the nose
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
In central cyanosis, reduced arterial oxygen saturation causes bluish discoloration of mucous membranes, particularly the tongue, as well as the lips and oral mucosa. Therefore, the tongue is never spared in true central cyanosis. In contrast, peripheral cyanosis may affect the nail beds, fingers, toes, and ear lobules while the tongue remains pink because arterial oxygenation is relatively preserved. This distinction is clinically useful: central cyanosis indicates systemic arterial desaturation, whereas peripheral cyanosis can result from reduced peripheral blood flow or vasoconstriction. Among the options, the tongue is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Central cyanosis → tongue and oral mucosa involved.

  • Peripheral cyanosis → extremities, nail beds, ear lobules.

  • Tongue usually remains pink in isolated peripheral cyanosis.

  • Central cyanosis indicates reduced arterial O₂ saturation.

  • Causes include severe lung disease, right-to-left shunts, and abnormal hemoglobin states.

Exam Pearl:
Central cyanosis never spares the tongue; a blue tongue strongly suggests central cyanosis.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৪৫) Renal blood flow is..........% of total cardiac output ?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The kidneys receive a remarkably high proportion of cardiac output, approximately 20–25% in a healthy adult at rest. Renal blood flow is around 1.1–1.2 L/min, while cardiac output is approximately 5 L/min. Therefore, the standard exam value is about 20% of total cardiac output. This high blood flow is primarily required for glomerular filtration and regulation of body fluid composition, rather than simply for the metabolic needs of renal tissue. The kidneys also receive a large proportion of their blood flow through the renal cortex, where most glomeruli are located.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Renal blood flow ≈ 20–25% of cardiac output.

  • Approximate renal blood flow → 1.1–1.2 L/min.

  • Renal plasma flow → approximately 600–700 mL/min.

  • Most renal blood flow goes to the cortex.

  • High renal blood flow supports glomerular filtration and homeostasis.

Exam Pearl:
Kidneys receive about 20% of cardiac output at rest.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৪৬) Which junctional tissue has highest speed of conduction?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Among the listed cardiac conducting tissues, Purkinje fibers have the highest conduction velocity, approximately 2–4 m/s. Their rapid conduction ensures that the electrical impulse reaches the ventricular myocardium almost simultaneously, producing coordinated ventricular contraction. The SAN has a slower conduction velocity and functions primarily as the pacemaker. The AV node (AVN) has the slowest conduction velocity in the cardiac conduction system, creating the physiological AV nodal delay that allows time for ventricular filling. The AV bundle (bundle of His) conducts faster than the AV node but slower than Purkinje fibers. Therefore, Purkinje fibers are the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Purkinje fibers → fastest conduction.

  • AV node → slowest conduction.

  • AV nodal delay → allows ventricular filling.

  • SAN → primary pacemaker.

  • Purkinje conduction velocity → approximately 2–4 m/s.

Exam Pearl:
Fastest conduction = Purkinje fibers; slowest conduction = AV node.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৪৭) Positive Benedict test indicates that their might be a problem in.......?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
A positive Benedict’s test indicates the presence of reducing substances, particularly glucose, in urine. Normally, almost all filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) through sodium-glucose cotransporters. Therefore, glycosuria can occur when the filtered glucose load exceeds the renal threshold, as in diabetes mellitus, or when proximal tubular glucose reabsorption is impaired, as in Fanconi syndrome. Thus, among the given nephron segments, the PCT is the most relevant site of abnormality. However, Benedict’s test is not specific for glucose and can also detect other reducing substances such as fructose and galactose.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Glucose reabsorption → mainly PCT.

  • Transporter → SGLT2 predominantly in early PCT.

  • Glycosuria → diabetes mellitus or proximal tubular dysfunction.

  • Fanconi syndrome → generalized PCT reabsorptive defect.

  • Benedict’s test detects reducing sugars, not glucose specifically.

Exam Pearl:
Benedict-positive urine with glycosuria points toward a PCT problem or an increased filtered glucose load.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৪৮) Meissner's plexus lies in which layer of GIT?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Meissner’s plexus, also called the submucosal plexus, is located within the submucosa of the gastrointestinal tract. It primarily regulates glandular secretion, mucosal blood flow, and local muscular activity. In contrast, Auerbach’s (myenteric) plexus lies between the inner circular and outer longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa and mainly regulates GI motility and peristalsis. The enteric nervous system therefore has two major plexuses: Meissner’s in the submucosa and Auerbach’s in the muscularis externa.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Meissner’s plexus → submucosa.

  • Main function → secretion and mucosal blood flow.

  • Auerbach’s plexus → muscularis externa.

  • Auerbach’s main function → GI motility.

  • Both are components of the enteric nervous system.

Exam Pearl:
Meissner = Submucosa; Auerbach = Muscularis externa.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৪৯) What is the duration of maximum ejection period of cardiac cycle?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The maximum ejection phase occurs during ventricular systole after the ventricular pressure exceeds the pressure in the aorta and pulmonary artery, causing the semilunar valves to open. In a normal cardiac cycle at a heart rate of about 75/min, ventricular ejection lasts approximately 0.25 seconds, and the maximum (rapid) ejection period is approximately 0.11 seconds. It is followed by the reduced ejection period. The remaining options represent shorter intervals associated with other phases of the cardiac cycle. Therefore, 0.11 seconds is the accepted examination answer for the maximum ejection period.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Maximum/rapid ejection → approximately 0.11 s.

  • Total ventricular ejection → approximately 0.25 s.

  • Ventricular systole → approximately 0.3 s.

  • Isovolumetric contraction → approximately 0.05 s.

  • Isovolumetric relaxation → approximately 0.08 s.

Exam Pearl:
Maximum ejection period ≈ 0.11 seconds.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৫০) Which one of following is transcellular fluid?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Transcellular fluid is a specialized component of extracellular fluid (ECF) that is separated from the rest of the ECF by epithelial cell layers. Examples include cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), synovial fluid, pleural fluid, peritoneal fluid, and aqueous humor. Therefore, CSF is the correct answer. Interstitial fluid and plasma are the major components of ECF but are not classified as transcellular fluid. Intracellular fluid (ICF) is the fluid contained within cells and is a separate major body-fluid compartment.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • CSF → transcellular fluid.

  • Transcellular fluid → specialized part of ECF.

  • Plasma → ECF.

  • Interstitial fluid → ECF.

  • ICF → fluid inside cells.

Exam Pearl:
CSF is a classic example of transcellular fluid.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৫১) Which indicates the beginning of ventricular filling?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The third heart sound (S3) is associated with the rapid phase of ventricular filling during early diastole. It occurs shortly after S2, when the AV valves have opened and blood flows rapidly from the atria into the ventricles. S1 marks the beginning of ventricular systole and is produced by closure of the AV valves. S2 marks the beginning of ventricular diastole and results from closure of the semilunar valves. Although ventricular filling technically begins after S2 when the AV valves open, S3 is the heart sound classically associated with rapid ventricular filling. Therefore, for this MCQ, S3 is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • S1 → AV valve closure → beginning of ventricular systole.

  • S2 → semilunar valve closure → beginning of ventricular diastole.

  • S3 → rapid ventricular filling.

  • S4 → atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle.

  • S3 may be physiological in children and young adults.

Exam Pearl:
S3 = rapid ventricular filling; S4 = atrial contraction.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৫২) Countercurrent blood flow is absent in.......?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
A countercurrent arrangement occurs when two fluids flow in opposite directions, allowing efficient exchange between them. In the kidney, the vasa recta form a countercurrent exchange system that helps maintain the medullary osmotic gradient. In the testis, the pampiniform plexus acts as a countercurrent heat-exchange system, helping maintain a lower testicular temperature. In intestinal villi, countercurrent blood flow contributes to the regulation of the villous oxygen gradient and can produce a physiological oxygen shunt. In contrast, pulmonary gas exchange is classically described as crosscurrent, where pulmonary capillary blood flows across the alveolar air stream rather than in a true countercurrent direction.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Kidney → countercurrent exchange via vasa recta.

  • Testis → countercurrent heat exchange via pampiniform plexus.

  • Intestinal villi → countercurrent circulation.

  • Lung → crosscurrent, not countercurrent.

  • Crosscurrent exchange is important for efficient pulmonary gas exchange.

Exam Pearl:
Lung = crosscurrent exchange; kidney and testis = classic countercurrent systems.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৫৩) ECF volume is mainly maintained by......?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Extracellular fluid (ECF) volume is mainly regulated by the total body sodium content, because sodium is the major effective osmole of the ECF and water follows sodium. Aldosterone promotes sodium reabsorption, particularly in the distal nephron and collecting duct, thereby increasing ECF sodium and water retention. Although ADH is important for regulating water balance and plasma osmolality, it primarily controls water concentration, not the overall ECF volume. Oxytocin does not play a major role in ECF regulation, and prostaglandins have modulatory effects on renal blood flow and sodium handling. Therefore, among the given options, aldosterone is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • ECF volume is mainly determined by total body Na⁺.

  • Aldosterone → Na⁺ retention → water retention → ↑ ECF volume.

  • ADH → mainly regulates water balance/osmolality.

  • ANP → promotes Na⁺ and water excretion.

  • RAAS is a major system regulating ECF volume and blood pressure.

Exam Pearl:
ECF volume follows sodium: aldosterone retains Na⁺ and therefore expands ECF volume.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৫৪) Which is a positive inotropic agent?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Digoxin is a positive inotropic agent because it increases the force of cardiac muscle contraction. It inhibits the myocardial Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, increasing intracellular Na⁺ concentration. This reduces the activity of the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger, leading to increased intracellular Ca²⁺ availability for subsequent cardiac contractions. Digoxin therefore produces a positive inotropic effect and can be used in selected patients with heart failure. Beta blockers generally reduce myocardial contractility acutely (negative inotropy), while most calcium channel blockers, particularly verapamil and diltiazem, have negative inotropic effects. Amiodarone is primarily an antiarrhythmic drug and is not classified as a positive inotrope.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Digoxin → positive inotropy.

  • Mechanism → inhibits Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase.

  • Result → ↑ intracellular Ca²⁺ → ↑ contractility.

  • Beta blockers → generally negative inotropy.

  • Verapamil/diltiazem → negative inotropy.

  • Digoxin also increases vagal activity → ↓ AV conduction.

Exam Pearl:
Digoxin increases contractility by increasing intracellular Ca²⁺.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৫৫) Plasma osmolarity is mainly exerted by......?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Plasma osmolarity is determined mainly by sodium and its accompanying anions, particularly NaCl. Sodium is the major effective osmole in the extracellular fluid and accounts for the largest contribution to plasma osmolarity. Although glucose and proteins such as albumin contribute to plasma osmolarity, their contribution under normal conditions is much smaller. Albumin is especially important for maintaining plasma colloid oncotic pressure, rather than overall osmolarity. Bicarbonate also contributes to plasma osmolality but is less important than sodium salts. Therefore, among the given options, NaCl is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Main determinant of plasma osmolarity → Na⁺ and accompanying anions.

  • Na⁺ is the major ECF osmole.

  • Albumin → major determinant of plasma oncotic pressure.

  • Normal plasma osmolarity ≈ 285–295 mOsm/kg.

  • Glucose contributes significantly only when markedly elevated.

Exam Pearl:
Na⁺ salts, especially NaCl, are the major contributors to plasma osmolarity.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৫৬) Which digestive juice has least pH?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Gastric juice has the lowest pH among the given digestive secretions, typically around 1–3, because of its high concentration of hydrochloric acid (HCl) secreted by gastric parietal cells. The acidic environment is essential for pepsin activation, protein digestion, and destruction of many ingested microorganisms. Saliva is approximately pH 6–7, pancreatic juice is strongly alkaline (around pH 7.5–8.5) due to bicarbonate secretion, and succus entericus is generally near neutral to slightly alkaline. Therefore, gastric juice has the least (lowest) pH.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Gastric juice → pH 1–3.

  • Saliva → approximately pH 6–7.

  • Pancreatic juice → approximately pH 7.5–8.5.

  • Gastric HCl → secreted by parietal cells.

  • Pepsinogen → activated to pepsin in acidic pH.

Exam Pearl:
Lowest pH among digestive juices = gastric juice (≈1–3).

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৫৭) Which indicates the cardiac output?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Pulse pressure (PP) is the difference between systolic and diastolic blood pressure and is influenced mainly by stroke volume and arterial compliance. Because cardiac output is determined by heart rate and stroke volume, an increase in stroke volume generally increases pulse pressure. Thus, among the given options, pulse pressure is considered the best indicator of cardiac output/stroke volume. Systolic pressure and diastolic pressure are influenced by several factors, including peripheral resistance and arterial compliance. Mean arterial pressure is more closely related to the pressure required to drive systemic blood flow and depends on cardiac output and systemic vascular resistance, rather than directly indicating cardiac output.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Pulse pressure = SBP − DBP.

  • Pulse pressure mainly reflects stroke volume and arterial compliance.

  • Cardiac output = HR × SV.

  • Mean arterial pressure ≈ DBP + 1/3 pulse pressure at normal heart rates.

  • Increased stroke volume → generally increased pulse pressure.

Exam Pearl:
Pulse pressure is the best option here as an indirect indicator of stroke volume, and therefore cardiac output.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৫৮) Which factor is responsible for shifting K ion out of the cell?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Exercise can shift K⁺ out of cells into the extracellular fluid, particularly during intense muscle activity. Repeated action potentials cause K⁺ efflux through voltage-gated K⁺ channels during repolarization, producing a transient rise in extracellular potassium. Aldosterone generally promotes K⁺ secretion by renal tubular cells and therefore lowers extracellular K⁺ rather than directly shifting K⁺ out of cells. Insulin promotes K⁺ uptake into cells through stimulation of Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Alkalosis generally causes K⁺ to shift into cells, tending to produce hypokalemia. Thus, exercise is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Exercise → K⁺ shifts out of muscle cells.

  • Insulin → K⁺ shifts into cells.

  • Alkalosis → generally K⁺ shifts into cells.

  • Aldosterone → increases renal K⁺ secretion.

  • Intense exercise can cause transient hyperkalemia.

Exam Pearl:
Exercise pushes K⁺ out of skeletal muscle cells; insulin pushes K⁺ into cells.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৫৯) Which is short term regulation of blood pressure?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The CNS ischemic response is a powerful short-term mechanism for blood pressure regulation, particularly during severe hypotension. When cerebral blood flow falls markedly, ischemia of the medullary vasomotor center causes accumulation of CO₂, H⁺, and other metabolites, producing intense sympathetic activation. This results in vasoconstriction, increased heart rate and contractility, and increased arterial blood pressure. It is considered an emergency mechanism and becomes particularly important when arterial pressure falls below approximately 60 mmHg. ADH, thirst, and ANF/ANP are primarily involved in longer-term regulation of blood volume and fluid balance rather than being the principal rapid blood-pressure mechanisms.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • CNS ischemic response → short-term emergency BP regulation.

  • Trigger → severe fall in cerebral perfusion.

  • Effect → intense sympathetic activation.

  • Produces → vasoconstriction and increased cardiac activity.

  • Baroreceptor reflex → another major rapid BP-regulating mechanism.

  • ADH and thirst → mainly longer-term volume regulation.

Exam Pearl:
CNS ischemic response = emergency short-term mechanism for maintaining arterial blood pressure.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৬০) Which digestive juice has most amount of daily secretion?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Among the given digestive secretions, gastric juice is classically described as having one of the highest daily volumes, approximately 2 L/day in adults. It is secreted by the gastric glands and contains hydrochloric acid, pepsinogen, intrinsic factor, mucus, and other components. Saliva is approximately 1–1.5 L/day, pancreatic juice approximately 1–1.5 L/day, and intestinal juice (succus entericus) is approximately 1–2 L/day. There is some variation between standard physiological estimates, particularly for intestinal secretion, so the question can be somewhat ambiguous. However, in conventional MBBS examination tables, gastric juice ≈ 2 L/day is generally accepted as the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Gastric juice → approximately 2 L/day.

  • Saliva → approximately 1–1.5 L/day.

  • Pancreatic juice → approximately 1–1.5 L/day.

  • Succus entericus → approximately 1–2 L/day.

  • Gastric HCl → secreted by parietal cells.

Exam Pearl:
For standard MCQs: Gastric juice ≈ 2 L/day is the usual answer for the highest daily digestive secretion.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৬১) Which is ECG change in hypokalemia?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The characteristic ECG changes of hypokalemia include ST-segment depression, flattening or inversion of the T wave, and prominent U waves. As potassium levels fall further, the PR interval may become prolonged and the QRS complex may widen. In contrast, tall, peaked T waves are characteristic of hyperkalemia, not hypokalemia. An absent P wave is also associated with severe hyperkalemia. Therefore, among the given options, ST depression is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hypokalemia → ST depression.

  • Hypokalemia → flat/inverted T wave.

  • Hypokalemia → prominent U wave.

  • Hyperkalemia → tall, peaked T waves.

  • Severe hyperkalemia → wide QRS, absent P waves.

Exam Pearl:
Hypokalemia = ST depression + prominent U wave; hyperkalemia = tall peaked T wave.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৬২) Which reflex increases heart rate?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The Bainbridge reflex is a physiological reflex that increases heart rate in response to increased venous return and stretching of the atrial walls. Increased atrial stretch activates stretch receptors, particularly near the venoatrial junctions, leading to increased sympathetic activity and reduced vagal activity, thereby increasing SA node firing and heart rate. In contrast, the baroreceptor reflex generally decreases heart rate when arterial blood pressure rises. The chemoreceptor reflex can increase heart rate during significant hypoxia or hypercapnia, but its primary cardiovascular effect is more complex. The Cushing reflex occurs in response to markedly increased intracranial pressure and classically produces hypertension with reflex bradycardia.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Bainbridge reflex → increased heart rate.

  • Stimulus → increased venous return/atrial stretch.

  • Baroreceptor reflex → mainly decreases HR when BP rises.

  • Cushing reflex → hypertension + bradycardia.

  • Bainbridge reflex helps prevent excessive venous congestion.

Exam Pearl:
Increased venous return → atrial stretch → Bainbridge reflex → increased heart rate.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৬৩) Which hormone exhibit permissive action?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Cortisol exhibits a classic permissive action by enhancing the effects of other hormones, particularly catecholamines. Cortisol increases the expression or responsiveness of α₁-adrenergic receptors in vascular smooth muscle, thereby allowing catecholamines to produce an adequate vasoconstrictor response and maintain normal blood pressure. Without sufficient cortisol, the vascular response to catecholamines is reduced, contributing to hypotension in adrenal insufficiency. Catecholamines themselves are major effector hormones rather than the classic example of a permissive hormone. Aldosterone primarily regulates sodium and potassium balance, while glucagon promotes hepatic glucose production. Therefore, cortisol is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Cortisol → permissive effect on catecholamines.

  • Cortisol ↑ α₁-adrenergic receptor responsiveness.

  • Helps maintain vascular tone and blood pressure.

  • Cortisol deficiency → reduced response to catecholamines → hypotension.

  • Permissive action means one hormone enhances the effect of another hormone.

Exam Pearl:
Cortisol permits catecholamines to exert their full vasoconstrictor effect.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৬৪) Proteolytic enzymes excludes.....?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Proteolytic enzymes digest proteins by hydrolyzing peptide bonds. Pepsin is a gastric protease that begins protein digestion in the stomach. Trypsin and chymotrypsin are pancreatic proteases that digest proteins and peptides in the small intestine. Ptyalin, also known as salivary amylase, is a carbohydrate-digesting enzyme that hydrolyzes starch into smaller carbohydrates such as maltose and dextrins. Therefore, ptyalin is not a proteolytic enzyme and is the correct answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Pepsin → protein digestion.

  • Trypsin → protein digestion.

  • Chymotrypsin → protein digestion.

  • Ptyalin (salivary amylase) → carbohydrate digestion.

  • Pepsin is secreted as pepsinogen by gastric chief cells.

Exam Pearl:
Ptyalin = salivary amylase = carbohydrate-digesting enzyme, not a protease.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৬৫) Which is physiological cause of bradycardia?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Sleep is a physiological cause of bradycardia because parasympathetic (vagal) activity predominates during sleep, particularly during non-REM sleep. Increased vagal tone reduces the firing rate of the SA node, resulting in a lower heart rate. In contrast, exercise normally causes tachycardia through increased sympathetic activity and reduced vagal tone. Strong emotions also commonly increase heart rate through sympathetic activation. Pregnancy is associated with an increased resting heart rate rather than physiological bradycardia. Therefore, among the given options, sleep is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Sleep → physiological bradycardia.

  • Exercise → tachycardia.

  • Emotion/stress → usually tachycardia.

  • Pregnancy → usually increased heart rate.

  • Increased vagal tone → decreased SA node firing.

Exam Pearl:
Sleep is a classic physiological cause of bradycardia due to increased vagal tone.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৬৬) Which one is function of dopamine?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
At low doses, dopamine acts predominantly on D₁ receptors, producing vasodilation, particularly in the renal, mesenteric, and coronary vascular beds. This can reduce systemic vascular resistance and consequently cause a decrease in diastolic blood pressure (DBP). Dopamine does not cause renal vasoconstriction at low doses. At higher doses, its effects become increasingly mediated by β₁ receptors (increased cardiac contractility) and then α₁ receptors (vasoconstriction and increased blood pressure). Therefore, among the given options, reduced DBP is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Low-dose dopamine → D₁ receptor activation → vasodilation.

  • D₁ effect → renal and mesenteric vasodilation.

  • Moderate dose → β₁ → increased cardiac contractility.

  • High dose → α₁ → vasoconstriction and increased BP.

  • Dopamine does not primarily cause renal vasoconstriction at low doses.

Exam Pearl:
Dopamine: low dose → D₁ vasodilation; moderate → β₁ cardiac stimulation; high → α₁ vasoconstriction.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৬৭) Which event occurs in the heart during Q wave production?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The Q wave is the first negative deflection of the QRS complex and represents the initial phase of ventricular depolarization, specifically the depolarization of the interventricular septum. Normally, the septum depolarizes from left to right, producing small Q waves in the lateral leads and small R waves in the right-sided precordial leads. The entire QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization, but the Q wave specifically corresponds to the initial septal activation. Atrial depolarization is represented by the P wave, while ventricular repolarization is represented by the T wave.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • P wave → atrial depolarization.

  • Q wave → initial septal depolarization.

  • QRS complex → ventricular depolarization.

  • T wave → ventricular repolarization.

  • Normal septal depolarization → left to right.

Exam Pearl:
Q wave = initial septal depolarization.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৬৮) Intrinsic factor of Castle is secreted by which cell of stomach?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Intrinsic factor (Castle’s intrinsic factor) is secreted by the parietal cells, also called oxyntic cells, of the stomach, particularly in the fundus and body. Intrinsic factor binds to vitamin B12 and is essential for its absorption in the terminal ileum. Deficiency of intrinsic factor, classically due to autoimmune destruction of parietal cells, causes impaired vitamin B12 absorption and can lead to pernicious anemia. Parietal cells also secrete hydrochloric acid (HCl). Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, G cells secrete gastrin, and mucous neck cells secrete mucus.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Oxyntic/parietal cell → HCl + intrinsic factor.

  • Intrinsic factor → required for vitamin B12 absorption.

  • B12–intrinsic factor complex → absorbed in terminal ileum.

  • G cell → gastrin.

  • Chief cell → pepsinogen.

Exam Pearl:
Intrinsic factor = parietal (oxyntic) cell = vitamin B12 absorption.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৬৯)  Which is an effect of noradrenaline?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Noradrenaline (norepinephrine) predominantly stimulates α₁ and β₁ adrenergic receptors. β₁-receptor stimulation in the heart produces positive inotropy, increasing the force of ventricular contraction. Noradrenaline also causes marked α₁-mediated vasoconstriction, increasing systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure. The resulting rise in blood pressure can trigger reflex bradycardia, but this is a secondary reflex effect rather than its direct cardiac action. Noradrenaline does not cause hypoglycemia. Therefore, increased force of contraction is the best single answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Noradrenaline → α₁ + β₁ predominant action.

  • β₁ → increased force of contraction.

  • α₁ → vasoconstriction.

  • ↑ BP from noradrenaline → may cause reflex bradycardia.

  • Adrenaline has a more prominent β₂-mediated vasodilator effect than noradrenaline.

Exam Pearl:
Noradrenaline directly increases cardiac contractility via β₁ receptors.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৭০) Which is not true about systemic circulation?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Systemic circulation carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle through the systemic arteries to essentially all tissues of the body and returns deoxygenated blood through the systemic veins to the right atrium. Unlike pulmonary circulation, systemic circulation is a high-pressure circulation, because it must generate sufficient pressure to perfuse the entire body, including organs distant from the heart. Therefore, “low pressure” is not a true feature of systemic circulation and is the correct answer. Pulmonary circulation, in contrast, is a low-pressure, low-resistance circulation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Systemic circulation → left ventricle → body → right atrium.

  • Systemic circulation → high pressure.

  • Pulmonary circulation → right ventricle → lungs → left atrium.

  • Pulmonary circulation → low pressure.

  • Systemic circulation has much higher vascular resistance than pulmonary circulation.

Exam Pearl:
Systemic = high pressure; pulmonary = low pressure.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৭১) ( In few references only glutamate & acetylcholine  are taken as excitatory, in other references 5HT & sub-P are also taken as excitatory. So this question is cancelled.) Which is an excitatory neurotransmitter?
৭২) Three basic stimuli for pancreatic secretion excludes.....?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The three major physiological stimuli for pancreatic exocrine secretion are acetylcholine (ACh), cholecystokinin (CCK), and secretin. ACh, released from vagal parasympathetic nerve endings, stimulates enzyme-rich pancreatic secretion. CCK, released from duodenal I cells in response to fats and amino acids, mainly stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion. Secretin, released from duodenal S cells in response to acidic chyme, primarily stimulates bicarbonate-rich fluid secretion from pancreatic duct cells. Gastrin can have some stimulatory effects on pancreatic secretion but is not considered one of the three basic physiological stimuli. Therefore, gastrin is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • 3 major pancreatic secretory stimuli → ACh + CCK + Secretin.

  • ACh → enzyme secretion.

  • CCK → enzyme-rich secretion.

  • Secretin → HCO₃⁻-rich secretion.

  • Gastrin → not one of the three principal stimuli.

Exam Pearl:
Pancreatic secretion: ACh + CCK + secretin; gastrin is the excluded option.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৭৩) Which is a vasodilator agent?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Bradykinin is a potent endogenous vasodilator. It acts mainly on B₂ receptors on vascular endothelial cells, stimulating the release of nitric oxide (NO) and prostacyclin, which relax vascular smooth muscle and increase local blood flow. It also increases vascular permeability and contributes to pain and inflammation. Norepinephrine predominantly causes vasoconstriction through α₁ receptors, while vasopressin (ADH) causes potent vasoconstriction through V₁ receptors. Epinephrine is dose-dependent: at low concentrations, β₂-mediated vasodilation can occur, while at higher concentrations α₁-mediated vasoconstriction predominates. Nevertheless, among the given options, bradykinin is the clearest and most accepted vasodilator.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Bradykinin → potent vasodilation.

  • Bradykinin → B₂ receptor → NO/prostacyclin.

  • Norepinephrine → mainly α₁ vasoconstriction.

  • Vasopressin → V₁ vasoconstriction.

  • Epinephrine → β₂ vasodilation at low doses.

Exam Pearl:
Bradykinin is a classic endogenous vasodilator.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৭৪) Which one is not the properties of synapse?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
A synapse is generally a one-way conduction junction because neurotransmitter release occurs from the presynaptic terminal, while receptors are located on the postsynaptic membrane. Therefore, impulses normally pass only from the presynaptic neuron to the postsynaptic neuron. Summation is an important property of synapses and may be temporal or spatial. Occlusion can occur when simultaneous stimulation of different presynaptic inputs produces a smaller-than-expected response due to shared postsynaptic neurons. Synapses can also undergo fatigue, mainly because of depletion of neurotransmitter stores during prolonged repetitive stimulation. Hence, two-way conduction is not a property of synapses.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Synapse → one-way conduction.

  • Synapse → summation.

  • Synapse → occlusion.

  • Synapse → fatigue.

  • One-way transmission is due to polarization of synaptic structure.

Exam Pearl:
