Synapse conducts impulses in one direction only: presynaptic → postsynaptic.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৭৫) Which is conducting vessel?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Blood vessels are functionally classified as conducting, distributing, resistance, exchange, and capacitance vessels. The aorta and other large elastic arteries are conducting vessels because they transport blood away from the heart to the distributing arteries. Their abundant elastic tissue allows them to expand during ventricular systole and recoil during diastole, helping maintain continuous blood flow. Arterioles are resistance vessels and are the major site of regulation of systemic vascular resistance. Capillaries are exchange vessels, while veins, including the vena cava, are mainly capacitance vessels that store a large proportion of the circulating blood volume. Therefore, aorta is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Aorta/large elastic arteries → conducting vessels.

  • Arteries → mainly distributing vessels.

  • Arterioles → resistance vessels.

  • Capillaries → exchange vessels.

  • Veins/vena cava → capacitance vessels.

Exam Pearl:
Aorta = conducting vessel; arteriole = resistance vessel; capillary = exchange vessel.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৭৬) What is the source of secretion of CCK?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Cholecystokinin (CCK) is secreted mainly by I cells located in the mucosa of the duodenum and jejunum. Its release is stimulated particularly by fatty acids and amino acids entering the small intestine. CCK promotes pancreatic enzyme secretion, causes gallbladder contraction, and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, facilitating delivery of bile and pancreatic enzymes into the duodenum. G cells secrete gastrin, while S cells secrete secretin. Therefore, I cell is the correct source of CCK.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • I cell → CCK

  • S cell → Secretin

  • G cell → Gastrin

  • CCK → gallbladder contraction + pancreatic enzyme secretion.

  • Secretin → pancreatic HCO₃⁻ secretion.

Exam Pearl:
I cell = CCK; S cell = secretin; G cell = gastrin.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৭৭) Which one is for pressure & vibration sensation?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors specialized for detecting deep pressure and vibration. They are particularly sensitive to high-frequency vibration and rapid changes in mechanical pressure. They are found mainly in the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissues, as well as around joints and other deeper structures. Free nerve endings primarily detect pain, temperature, and crude touch. Krause end bulbs are classically associated with cold sensation and are not the principal receptors for pressure and vibration. Hair follicle receptors detect movement of hairs and light touch. Therefore, Pacinian corpuscles are the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Pacinian corpuscle → deep pressure + vibration

  • Meissner corpuscle → fine/light touch

  • Free nerve endings → pain + temperature

  • Hair follicle receptors → hair movement/light touch

  • Pacinian corpuscles → rapidly adapting

Exam Pearl:
Pressure and vibration = Pacinian corpuscle.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৭৮) Which is example of obstructive shock?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Obstructive shock occurs when there is a mechanical obstruction to cardiac filling or blood outflow, resulting in reduced cardiac output despite adequate intravascular volume. Cardiac tamponade is a classic example: accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac increases intrapericardial pressure, compresses the cardiac chambers, particularly during diastole, and reduces venous return and ventricular filling. This leads to decreased stroke volume and cardiac output, causing hypotension and shock. Sepsis causes distributive shock, burns primarily cause hypovolemic shock due to fluid loss, and arrhythmias may cause cardiogenic shock by impairing cardiac output but are not classified as obstructive shock.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Obstructive shock → mechanical obstruction to filling or outflow.

  • Cardiac tamponade → obstructive shock.

  • Massive pulmonary embolism → obstructive shock.

  • Tension pneumothorax → obstructive shock.

  • Sepsis → distributive shock.

  • Severe burns → hypovolemic shock.

Exam Pearl:
Cardiac tamponade is a classic cause of obstructive shock.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৭৯) Which one is root value of knee jerk?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The knee jerk (patellar reflex) is a deep tendon reflex mediated predominantly by the L3–L4 spinal nerve roots, with L4 being the major root. Tapping the patellar tendon stretches the quadriceps muscle spindles, producing an afferent impulse through the femoral nerve to the spinal cord. The reflex arc then activates α-motor neurons supplying the quadriceps, causing knee extension. The L3–L4 roots are therefore the classic root values tested clinically. In contrast, the S1–S2 roots are mainly associated with the ankle jerk.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Knee jerk → L3–L4

  • Major root → L4

  • Nerve → femoral nerve

  • Ankle jerk → S1–S2, mainly S1

  • Knee jerk tests the L4 spinal segment clinically.

Exam Pearl:
Knee jerk = L3–L4 (mainly L4) via femoral nerve.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৮০) Which is the end product of starch digestion?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The final products of starch digestion are primarily glucose molecules. Starch is a polysaccharide composed mainly of glucose units linked by α-glycosidic bonds. Digestion begins in the mouth with salivary amylase (ptyalin) and continues in the small intestine with pancreatic amylase, producing smaller carbohydrates such as maltose, maltotriose, and α-limit dextrins. Brush-border enzymes, particularly maltase and α-dextrinase, ultimately break these down into glucose, which is then absorbed by intestinal enterocytes. Fructose and galactose are derived mainly from other dietary sugars rather than starch.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Starch → ultimately glucose.

  • Salivary amylase → begins starch digestion.

  • Pancreatic amylase → major intestinal starch digestion.

  • Maltase/α-dextrinase → final breakdown to glucose.

  • Sucrose → glucose + fructose.

  • Lactose → glucose + galactose.

Exam Pearl:
Starch is a glucose polymer; its final digestible product is glucose.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৮১) Which is increased after haemorrhage?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
After hemorrhage, blood volume and venous return decrease, leading to reduced stroke volume and a fall in arterial pressure. The decrease in arterial pressure reduces firing of baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch. This increases sympathetic activity and decreases parasympathetic activity, producing tachycardia, increased myocardial contractility, and peripheral vasoconstriction. Therefore, heart rate increases as an important compensatory response to hemorrhage. Cardiac output, blood pressure, and venous return generally decrease because of reduced circulating blood volume.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hemorrhage → ↓ blood volume

  • ↓ venous return → ↓ stroke volume

  • ↓ BP → ↓ baroreceptor firing

  • ↑ sympathetic activity → ↑ heart rate + vasoconstriction

  • Cardiac output → generally decreases

Exam Pearl:
Hemorrhage → baroreceptor reflex → tachycardia.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৮২) What is the feature of UMNL?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
A positive Babinski sign is a classic feature of an upper motor neuron lesion (UMNL). Damage to corticospinal pathways removes descending inhibitory control over spinal reflex circuits, producing hyperreflexia, increased muscle tone (spasticity), clonus, and an extensor plantar response (Babinski sign). In contrast, lower motor neuron lesions typically cause flaccid paralysis, hypotonia, reduced or absent deep tendon reflexes, and muscle wasting. Therefore, among the given options, a positive Babinski sign is the characteristic feature of UMNL.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • UMNL → spasticity

  • UMNL → hyperreflexia

  • UMNL → clonus may be present

  • UMNL → Babinski positive

  • LMNL → flaccidity + hyporeflexia/areflexia + wasting

Exam Pearl:
UMN lesion = spasticity + hyperreflexia + positive Babinski.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৮৩) Factors influencing gaseous transport across the respiratory membrane excludes....?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Gas transfer across the respiratory membrane follows Fick’s law of diffusion. The rate of diffusion is directly proportional to the surface area and the diffusion coefficient of the gas, and inversely proportional to the thickness of the respiratory membrane. Therefore, membrane thickness, surface area, and the diffusion coefficient are recognized factors influencing gaseous diffusion. Length of the membrane is not a standard determinant of gas diffusion across the respiratory membrane. Conditions such as pulmonary edema or fibrosis increase membrane thickness and impair diffusion, while emphysema decreases surface area and reduces gas exchange.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • ↑ Surface area → ↑ diffusion.

  • ↑ Diffusion coefficient → ↑ diffusion.

  • ↑ Membrane thickness → ↓ diffusion.

  • Respiratory membrane is normally very thin.

  • Emphysema → ↓ surface area → impaired diffusion.

Exam Pearl:
Fick’s law: diffusion depends on surface area, diffusion coefficient, and membrane thickness—not membrane length.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৮৪) What is the site of origin of hormone sensitive lipase?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) is an intracellular lipolytic enzyme found predominantly in adipocytes. It is responsible for mobilizing stored triglycerides by hydrolyzing stored lipid intermediates, particularly diacylglycerol, to release free fatty acids and glycerol. HSL activity is stimulated by catecholamines through β-adrenergic receptors → cAMP → protein kinase A, while insulin inhibits lipolysis. Although adipose triglyceride lipase initiates triglyceride breakdown, HSL is a major enzyme in hormone-regulated lipolysis. Therefore, the site of origin/source of HSL is the adipocyte.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • HSL → adipocytes.

  • Catecholamines → activate HSL.

  • Insulin → inhibits lipolysis.

  • β-receptor → cAMP → PKA → HSL activation.

  • HSL is important for mobilization of stored fat.

Exam Pearl:
Hormone-sensitive lipase = adipocyte enzyme responsible for hormone-regulated lipolysis.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৮৫) Referred pain is carried by which of the following?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Referred pain is typically carried by visceral afferent pain fibers, which are predominantly slow, unmyelinated C fibers. These fibers conduct dull, aching, poorly localized pain from visceral organs. In referred pain, visceral and somatic afferent fibers converge on common neurons in the spinal cord, and the CNS may incorrectly interpret the visceral pain as arising from a somatic structure sharing the same spinal segment. A-delta fibers are thinly myelinated and mainly carry fast, sharp, well-localized pain. B fibers are primarily autonomic preganglionic fibers, while A-alpha fibers mainly carry proprioceptive information and motor impulses.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Visceral pain → mainly C fibers.

  • Referred pain → C fibers.

  • C fibers → slow, dull, poorly localized pain.

  • A-delta → fast, sharp pain.

  • B fibers → preganglionic autonomic fibers.

Exam Pearl:
Referred visceral pain is mainly carried by slow, unmyelinated C fibers.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৮৬) The spirometer cannot be used in a direct way to measure which of the following?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
A spirometer measures the volume of air that can be moved into or out of the lungs. Therefore, it can directly measure tidal volume (TV), inspiratory reserve volume (IRV), and expiratory reserve volume (ERV). However, residual volume (RV) is the amount of air remaining in the lungs after maximal forced expiration. This air cannot be voluntarily expelled into the spirometer, so RV cannot be measured directly by simple spirometry. Consequently, capacities containing RV, such as functional residual capacity (FRC) and total lung capacity (TLC), also cannot be measured directly by spirometry.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Spirometry directly measures → TV, IRV, ERV.

  • RV → cannot be measured directly by spirometry.

  • FRC = ERV + RV → not directly measurable.

  • TLC = VC + RV → not directly measurable.

  • RV can be measured using helium dilution, nitrogen washout, or body plethysmography.

Exam Pearl:
Spirometer cannot measure any lung volume containing residual volume; the classic answer is RV.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৮৭) Posterior column transmits........?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The posterior (dorsal) column of the spinal cord carries sensory information related to fine touch, vibration, conscious proprioception, and two-point discrimination. It consists mainly of the fasciculus gracilis (tract of Goll) and fasciculus cuneatus (tract of Burdach). The tract of Goll carries these sensations from the lower trunk and lower limbs. The other listed tracts are ascending pathways located outside the posterior column. The ventral spinocerebellar tract carries unconscious proprioceptive information, while spinoreticular and spino-olivary pathways are separate ascending pathways.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Posterior column → fine touch + vibration + conscious proprioception

  • Tract of Goll (gracilis) → lower body

  • Tract of Burdach (cuneatus) → upper body

  • Posterior column fibers synapse in gracile/cuneate nuclei in medulla.

  • Dorsal column pathway crosses in the medulla.

Exam Pearl:
Posterior column = Goll + Burdach; Goll carries sensations from the lower limb and lower trunk.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৮৮) Which movement occurs in large intestine?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The characteristic movement of the large intestine is haustration, produced by contractions of the taeniae coli and circular muscle. These contractions create sac-like pouches called haustra and facilitate mixing and slow movement of colonic contents, allowing absorption of water and electrolytes. The colon also exhibits peristaltic movements and powerful mass movements, but haustration is the characteristic movement classically associated with the large intestine in physiology MCQs. Segmental contractions and pendular movements are more commonly associated with intestinal mixing, particularly in the small intestine.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Large intestine → haustration + mass movements.

  • Haustra → sac-like pouches of the colon.

  • Mass movements → propel fecal material toward rectum.

  • Small intestine → segmentation and peristalsis.

  • Taeniae coli contribute to haustral formation.

Exam Pearl:
Characteristic movement of the large intestine = haustration.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৮৯) VC = ?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Vital capacity (VC) is the maximum volume of air that can be exhaled after a maximal inspiration. It consists of three components: inspiratory reserve volume (IRV), tidal volume (TV), and expiratory reserve volume (ERV). Therefore:

VC = IRV + TV + ERV

Residual volume (RV) is not included because it remains in the lungs even after maximal expiration. Consequently, total lung capacity (TLC) is VC + RV.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • VC = IRV + TV + ERV

  • TLC = VC + RV

  • FRC = ERV + RV

  • IC = TV + IRV

  • RV cannot be measured directly by simple spirometry.

Exam Pearl:
Vital Capacity = IRV + TV + ERV.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৯০) Which is not a feature of Extra Pyramidal Lesion?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Extrapyramidal lesions involve the basal ganglia and characteristically produce abnormalities of muscle tone and involuntary movement, rather than primary weakness. Typical features include rigidity, tremor, and hypokinesia/bradykinesia, as seen in Parkinsonism. Rigidity reflects increased muscle tone, while tremor and hypokinesia result from dysfunction of basal ganglia motor circuits. Polyneuropathy is a disorder of multiple peripheral nerves and is not a feature of extrapyramidal lesions. It commonly causes sensory symptoms, distal weakness, reduced reflexes, and muscle wasting. Therefore, polyneuropathy is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Extrapyramidal lesion → rigidity

  • → Tremor

  • → Hypokinesia/bradykinesia

  • → Abnormal involuntary movements may occur.

  • Polyneuropathy → peripheral nerve disorder, not extrapyramidal.

Exam Pearl:
Basal ganglia/extrapyramidal lesion = rigidity + tremor + hypokinesia; polyneuropathy is not a feature.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৯১) What is the value of residual volume?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Residual volume (RV) is the volume of air that remains in the lungs after maximum forced expiration. Its normal value is approximately 1200 mL in a healthy adult. RV is important because it prevents complete collapse of the alveoli and allows continuous gas exchange between breaths. It cannot be measured directly by simple spirometry, because the residual air cannot be expelled into the spirometer. RV can be measured indirectly using techniques such as helium dilution, nitrogen washout, or body plethysmography.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • RV ≈ 1200 mL

  • TV ≈ 500 mL

  • IRV ≈ 3000 mL

  • ERV ≈ 1100 mL

  • RV cannot be measured by simple spirometry.

Exam Pearl:
Residual volume = approximately 1200 mL.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৯২) Which of the following is fructose transporter?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
GLUT5 is the principal transporter responsible for fructose absorption across the apical membrane of small intestinal enterocytes. It facilitates fructose entry from the intestinal lumen by facilitated diffusion. After entering the enterocyte, fructose exits across the basolateral membrane mainly via GLUT2 into the portal circulation. GLUT2 also transports glucose and galactose, while GLUT1 and GLUT3 are primarily important for glucose transport, particularly in tissues with high glucose requirements. Therefore, GLUT5 is the best answer for the fructose transporter.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • GLUT5 → fructose

  • GLUT2 → glucose, galactose, fructose; basolateral intestinal transporter

  • GLUT1 → glucose; widely distributed

  • GLUT3 → glucose; especially neurons

  • Fructose absorption → GLUT5

Exam Pearl:
GLUT5 = fructose transporter.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৯৩) Which one is stimulation for aldosterone secretion?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Hemorrhage stimulates aldosterone secretion primarily by reducing circulating blood volume and renal perfusion, activating the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS). Reduced renal perfusion increases renin release, leading to formation of angiotensin II, which directly stimulates aldosterone secretion from the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex. Aldosterone promotes Na⁺ and water reabsorption and K⁺ excretion, helping restore extracellular fluid volume and blood pressure. In contrast, hyperkalemia, not hypokalemia, directly stimulates aldosterone secretion. Hypernatremia generally suppresses RAAS, while the supine position is not a primary stimulus for aldosterone secretion.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hemorrhage → ↑ RAAS → ↑ aldosterone

  • Hyperkalemia → direct ↑ aldosterone

  • Hypokalemia → ↓ aldosterone

  • Angiotensin II → major RAAS stimulus for aldosterone

  • Aldosterone → Na⁺ retention + K⁺ excretion

Exam Pearl:
Hemorrhage stimulates aldosterone via RAAS activation.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৯৪) GH is inhibited by......?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Free fatty acids (FFAs) inhibit growth hormone (GH) secretion. Elevated plasma FFAs exert a negative effect on GH release, and increased circulating FFAs can suppress the normal pulsatile secretion of GH. In contrast, hypoglycemia is a potent stimulus for GH secretion, as GH helps counteract low blood glucose. Exercise also stimulates GH release. GH secretion is particularly increased during slow-wave (deep) sleep, which occurs during NREM sleep, especially stages 3 and 4. Therefore, among the given options, free fatty acid is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • ↑ Free fatty acids → ↓ GH

  • Hypoglycemia → ↑ GH

  • Exercise → ↑ GH

  • Deep NREM sleep → ↑ GH

  • Somatostatin → inhibits GH secretion

Exam Pearl:
Free fatty acids inhibit GH; hypoglycemia, exercise, and deep sleep stimulate it.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৯৫) Where venous admixture of blood occurs?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Venous admixture refers to the addition of a small amount of deoxygenated blood to oxygenated arterial blood. In the heart, this occurs mainly through the venae cordis minimae (Thebesian veins), which drain directly into the cardiac chambers, especially the left ventricle. This deoxygenated blood mixes with oxygenated blood and contributes to the normal physiological venous admixture, explaining why arterial PO₂ is slightly lower than alveolar PO₂.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Venae cordis minimae (Thebesian veins) → venous admixture

  • Drain directly into cardiac chambers.

  • Physiological shunt also includes bronchial circulation → pulmonary veins.

  • Normal arterial blood is therefore not 100% oxygen-saturated.

Exam Pearl:
Venous admixture in systemic arterial blood → Thebesian veins (venae cordis minimae).

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৯৬) D cell of pancreas secretes........?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The D (delta) cells of the pancreatic islets secrete somatostatin. Somatostatin has an inhibitory effect on pancreatic and gastrointestinal functions, including inhibition of insulin and glucagon secretion and reduction of gastrointestinal secretions and motility.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • β-cell → Insulin

  • α-cell → Glucagon

  • δ-cell → Somatostatin

  • PP/F-cell → Pancreatic polypeptide

Exam Pearl:
Pancreatic D (δ) cell = Somatostatin.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৯৭) Which isn't true about factors preventing collapse of lung?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The lungs are normally prevented from collapsing by several factors, including pulmonary surfactant, residual volume, and interdependence between adjacent alveoli. The intrapleural pressure is normally negative, not positive. This negative intrapleural pressure creates the transpulmonary pressure that keeps the lungs expanded. If intrapleural pressure becomes positive, as in tension pneumothorax, the lung may collapse.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Surfactant → ↓ surface tension → prevents alveolar collapse.

  • Residual volume → helps maintain alveolar patency.

  • Interdependence of alveoli → supports neighboring alveoli.

  • Negative intrapleural pressure → keeps lung expanded.

  • Positive intrapleural pressure → lung collapse.

Exam Pearl:
Normal intrapleural pressure is negative; positive intrapleural pressure promotes lung collapse.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৯৮) The value of normal anion gap is....mEq/L?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The normal anion gap (AG) is classically about 8–16 mEq/L when calculated without including potassium:

AG = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻)

It represents the concentration of unmeasured anions in plasma, mainly albumin, phosphate, sulfate, and organic acids. The reference range can vary slightly depending on the laboratory and analyzer; 8–12 mEq/L is also commonly cited with modern ion-selective electrodes. However, among the given options, 8–16 mEq/L is the standard exam answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Normal AG = 8–16 mEq/L (common exam range)

  • AG ↑ → high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis

  • Major unmeasured anion → albumin

  • Formula → Na − (Cl + HCO₃)

Exam Pearl:
Normal anion gap ≈ 8–16 mEq/L.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ৯৯) What is the main muscle of inspiration?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
The diaphragm is the main muscle of inspiration and accounts for most of the increase in thoracic volume during quiet breathing. When it contracts, it descends and becomes flatter, increasing the vertical diameter of the thoracic cavity and lowering intrathoracic pressure, allowing air to enter the lungs. The external intercostal muscles assist by increasing the anteroposterior and transverse dimensions of the thorax. Sternocleidomastoid and other accessory muscles become important during forced inspiration.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Main muscle of inspiration → diaphragm

  • External intercostals → assist inspiration

  • Sternocleidomastoid → accessory muscle of inspiration

  • Internal intercostals → mainly forced expiration

Exam Pearl:
Quiet inspiration = diaphragm.

Subject Final-02 Physiology.question: ১০০) Which is not a diabetogenic hormone?
Subject Final-02 Physiology.exp:
Diabetogenic hormones are hormones that oppose the actions of insulin and tend to increase blood glucose. Important diabetogenic hormones include glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol, and growth hormone; thyroid hormones can also increase glucose availability and contribute to hyperglycemia. ADH (vasopressin) is primarily involved in water balance and vasoconstriction and is not classically considered a diabetogenic hormone.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Glucagon → diabetogenic

  • Epinephrine → diabetogenic

  • Cortisol → diabetogenic

  • GH → diabetogenic

  • ADH → not diabetogenic

Exam Pearl:
ADH is not a diabetogenic hormone.
